statement: In people who use drugs in North America who were offered fentanyl test strips (studies from 2016 to 2023), how many used them varied widely with the setting and with what was counted. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017) that gave 93 young adults ten strips each, with training and naloxone, and paid them to come back, 62 of the 81 who returned at least two weeks later said they had used at least one (77 in 100; 62 of all 93, or 67 in 100, editors' calculation), a median of 3 strips, and 10 had used all ten; 58 in 100 had given strips to others. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), where staff offered a check to every client, about 1 in 100 visits included one (1,411 of 134,176 visits, by an unknown number of people). At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 of 732 clients (57 in 100) said they had used strips in the past 30 days. A scoping review of 91 studies to March 2023 relays documented use from 1 to 80 in 100 (median 19), against stated willingness of 43 to 85 in 100; it includes the Rhode Island pilot. A British Columbia take-home programme did not count the kits it handed out, so its rate of use is unknown. Use was self-reported or recorded by services, and was not checked. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: How many people use test strips when they are offered them depends a lot on the setting. In a paid research study, about 3 in 4 young adults who were given ten strips and came back said they had used at least one in the following weeks. At a supervised injection site that offered a check on every visit, about 1 visit in 100 included a check. Across many studies, use ranged from 1 to 80 in 100 people, well below the share who said they were willing. This is what people said or what services recorded; it was not checked.
population: People who use drugs offered fentanyl test strips in North America: young adults in a paid Rhode Island research pilot (2017); clients of a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); the studies in one scoping review (to March 2023); people using ten British Columbia harm-reduction sites (2019)
exposure: Being given fentanyl test strips to take away (ten each in the pilot, five per take-home kit in British Columbia) or being offered an on-site strip check at each visit
comparator: None (a description); stated willingness to use strips is set beside documented use
outcome: Self-reported or service-recorded use of at least one strip; number of strips used; giving strips to others
magnitude: Rhode Island pilot: 62/81 analysed used at least one strip (76.5%; Wilson 95% CI 66.2–84.4%, editors' calculation); 62/93 given strips (66.7%; 56.6–75.4%, editors' calculation); median 3 strips (IQR 1–6); 10 (12%) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated). Vancouver supervised injection site: 1,411 checks in 134,176 visits (1.05%, editors' calculation), 7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017; the printed average of 533 visits a day does not fit the total, so the share is about 1% or less. Strip-distributing sites, 2023: 414/732 (56.6%) reported past-30-day use at baseline. Scoping review (relayed, unappraised): documented use 1–80% (median 19%); willingness 43–85% (five studies).

evidence.extracted: Rhode Island pilot: young adults aged 18 to 35 who reported heroin use, cocaine use, injection or buying pills on the street in the past 30 days were recruited through advertisements, fliers, word of mouth and an earlier study; at the first visit each watched training videos and received 10 single-use BTNX fentanyl urine strips for personal use, written instructions, overdose education and an intranasal naloxone kit. 93 completed the baseline interview, 83 (89.2%) returned for a second visit at least two weeks later and 81 were analysed; visits were paid $25 and $50.

At follow-up 62 of the 81 analysed (77%) reported using at least one of the strips provided, a median of 3 strips (IQR 1–6); 10 participants (12%) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated). Strip use and results were self-reported and not verified, and reasons for not using strips (23%) were not asked. Editors' calculation: 62 of 81 is 76.5% (Wilson 95% CI 66.2–84.4%); counting all 93 given strips, 62 of 93 is 66.7% (56.6–75.4%).

evidence.extracted: At Insite, a supervised injection facility in Vancouver, staff offered every client a fentanyl strip check on entering the injection room (before or after use, as the client chose). From 7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017, 1411 of 134,176 visits (1%) included a check, a daily average of 4.0 (range 0–27). The records were anonymous, so the number of people and of repeat checks is unknown; the same paragraph's average of 533 visits a day does not fit the total (card reporting issue), so the share is about 1% or less.

evidence.extracted: At 14 community organizations that hand out strips in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (recruited May to December 2023), 414 of 732 analysed participants (56.6%) said they had used fentanyl test strips in the 30 days before the baseline survey; the authors call this higher than the median uptake of 19% in a scoping review and link it to recruitment at sites that hand out strips.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods › Data sources and searches; Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community, 1st paragraph; Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Scoping review of 91 articles on fentanyl test strips (three databases searched on March 7, 2023; English only; mostly North American; no randomized trials; included studies not appraised): stated willingness to use strips ranged from 43% to 85% in five studies, while documented use ranged from 1% to 80% (median 19%; per-study values in a supplement not read).

evidence.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS distribution as a public health intervention, 1st paragraph; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Most distribution programmes report how many strips were handed out, and few report a change in strip use. Table 3 as relayed: 62 of 93 young adults given 10 free strips returned 2–4 weeks later having used at least one (Goldman 2019); 57 of 103 female sex workers in Baltimore given 5 strips returned and reported using at least one (Park 2020); use of 70% in Baltimore and 77% in Delaware after 17,000 strips were handed out over 7 months (Park 2021); 23 emergency department patients were offered strips, 18 accepted and 16 took them home (Lima 2022). Editors' observation: the Goldman 2019 counts are those of the Rhode Island pilot (Krieger et al., 2018), so that row is the same study.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Survey tools and testing kits, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Take-home kits of five strips were handed out with brief peer training at ten British Columbia harm-reduction sites from April to July 2019; no contact or demographic details were collected when kits were handed out and kits not returned were not followed up, so how many kits were used is unknown; 336 results sheets were returned.

risk_of_bias.note: Use was self-reported and unverified in the pilot (a paid convenience sample), the supervised injection site counted visits, not people, and the review relays unappraised figures.

inconsistency.note: From about 1 in 100 visits to 77 in 100 people, and 1 to 80 in 100 across the review's studies; partly explained by what was counted (people over a few weeks against visits) and by setting, partly not.

indirectness.note: North American services and a paid research pilot with training and naloxone; whether people offered strips elsewhere, or outside research and services, would use them as often is not known.

imprecision.note: The pilot's 62 of 81 has an interval of 66 to 84 in 100; the spread across settings matters more than the precision of any one study.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim; observational, starts low; risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness each take a level: very low. Counted once: the review's Goldman 2019 row (62 of 93) and its Rhode Island cohort (its ref. 70) are the same pilot as Krieger et al. (the counts match; editors' reading), and the review's Vancouver overdose prevention site study is Karamouzian et al. Status mixed: the shares differ more than the settings and measures fully explain.
